questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: a web search agent, a document analysis agent, a synthesis agent and a report generation agent. The system produces comprehensive, cited research reports.
questions.stem: The team registers four AgentDefinitions (search, analysis, synthesis, report) in the coordinator's options and writes a coordinator system prompt that tells it to delegate every research step. In testing, the coordinator never delegates and answers from its own knowledge. A configuration review shows that the coordinator's allowedTools lists only WebSearch, WebFetch and Read: the subagent-spawning Task tool is not in it. What is the MOST direct fix?

options.text: Rewrite each AgentDefinition description so it states more forcefully when the coordinator must hand work to that subagent.
Add "Task" to the coordinator's allowedTools so that the coordinator can actually invoke the subagents that are already defined.
Add few-shot examples to the coordinator prompt that show complete delegation exchanges with each of the four subagents.
Move the coordinator to a larger, more capable model so it reliably recognizes when a request needs delegation.

questions.explanation: Subagents are spawned through the **Task tool**. Defining subagents is not enough: the coordinator's `allowedTools` must include `"Task"`, otherwise it has no permitted way to delegate. The configuration review is the decisive clue: this is a tool-configuration gap, not a prompting or capability problem. (Version note: current docs name the tool `Agent` in `tool_use` blocks, while the `system:init` tools list still shows `Task` and `Task(...)` references still work as aliases. Today's SDK also separates pre-approving a tool (`allowedTools`) from removing it (`disallowedTools`). The exam guide frames this as "allowedTools must include Task", so answer that way on the exam.)

whyWrong.A: Descriptions help the coordinator choose *which* subagent to use, but no description can make it call a tool it does not have.
whyWrong.C: Few-shot examples shape behavior only when the behavior is possible; without the Task tool the model still cannot delegate.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model does not add tools. The failure is a missing capability in the configuration, not weak reasoning.

questions.mindset: When a tool-driven behavior never happens, check the configuration that grants the tool before tuning the prompt.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: a web search agent, a document analysis agent, a synthesis agent and a report generation agent. The system produces comprehensive, cited research reports.
questions.stem: After the search and analysis subagents finish, the coordinator spawns the synthesis subagent with the prompt "Synthesize the findings gathered so far into a structured summary with citations." The synthesis output is generic, cites almost nothing and sometimes says "based on the earlier discussion." Logs confirm that the search and analysis subagents returned rich, well-sourced results to the coordinator. What should the architect change?

options.text: Add a line to the synthesis AgentDefinition prompt stating that the search and analysis results from this session are available and must be used.
Give the synthesis subagent the web search and document tools so it can gather the evidence it needs on its own.
Raise the synthesis subagent's maxTurns so it has enough turns to locate the earlier findings before it writes.
Put the complete search results and document analysis outputs directly into the Task prompt sent to the synthesis subagent.

questions.explanation: A standard subagent runs with **isolated context**: it does not inherit the coordinator's conversation, tool results or memory. The Task prompt is the only channel from parent to subagent, so the coordinator must pass the complete prior findings (search results plus analysis outputs) explicitly in that prompt. This is exactly the exam guide's example of context passing to a synthesis subagent.

whyWrong.A: An instruction cannot reference data that was never passed. The results are not in the subagent's context, so telling it they are "available" only invites more hallucinated references to an "earlier discussion".
whyWrong.B: This makes the synthesis agent redo work already done, wastes tokens and blurs role boundaries, and it still never sees the findings that were already gathered.
whyWrong.C: More turns do not create access to data the subagent was never given. The findings are not anywhere it can look.

questions.mindset: A subagent only knows what you put in its prompt: pass the findings, not a reference to them.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: a web search agent, a document analysis agent, a synthesis agent and a report generation agent. The system produces comprehensive, cited research reports.
questions.stem: The team is writing an AgentDefinition for each of the four subagents and wants to be sure it understands what the main fields do. Which TWO statements about AgentDefinition fields are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Omitting the tools field gives the subagent no tools at all, so every tool it needs has to be listed explicitly.
The description is natural-language guidance that the coordinator uses to decide when to hand work to that subagent.
The prompt field is appended to the coordinator's system prompt, so the coordinator and subagent share one set of instructions.
The prompt field becomes the subagent's own system prompt, defining its role, expertise and constraints for its work.
The tools field can only add tools on top of the coordinator's set; it cannot take away any tool the coordinator has.

questions.explanation: An `AgentDefinition` has two required fields. **`description`** says, in plain language, when the subagent should be used; the coordinator matches tasks against it to decide whether and where to delegate (B). **`prompt`** is the subagent's **own system prompt**: its role, expertise and constraints (D). The optional `tools` field restricts the subagent to the listed tools; leaving it out means the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents.

whyWrong.A: It is the reverse. Omitting `tools` means the subagent inherits every tool available to subagents. Listing tools is how you restrict it.
whyWrong.C: The subagent's prompt is not merged into the coordinator's. Each agent has its own system prompt, and a standard subagent does not receive the coordinator's system prompt either.
whyWrong.E: The `tools` field is an allowlist that limits the subagent to exactly those tools, for example `["Read", "Grep", "Glob"]` for a read-only reviewer. Restricting tools is one of its main purposes.

questions.mindset: Description decides when a subagent is chosen, prompt decides how it behaves, tools decide what it can do.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: a web search agent, a document analysis agent, a synthesis agent and a report generation agent. The system produces comprehensive, cited research reports.
questions.stem: For each query, the coordinator calls the web search subagent, waits for it to return, and only in its next turn calls the document analysis subagent. The two tasks do not depend on each other, and end-to-end latency is too high. With the smallest change to the existing architecture, how should the architect reduce latency?

options.text: Have the coordinator emit both Task tool calls in a single response so the two independent subagents run in parallel.
Merge the search and document analysis subagents into one subagent that handles both kinds of work in a single pass.
Give the coordinator the search and document tools directly so it can do the work without spawning any subagents.
Run each subagent as a separate service behind a message queue and have the coordinator poll the queue for results.

questions.explanation: Parallel subagents come from **emitting multiple Task tool calls in one coordinator response**, not from spreading them across turns. Anthropic's research system reports that parallelization (the lead agent starting subagents in parallel, and subagents calling tools in parallel) cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries. This keeps the current coordinator-subagent design and only changes how delegation is issued.

whyWrong.B: Merging the agents gives up specialization and scoped tools. The work inside the merged agent still runs one step after another.
whyWrong.C: This drops the multi-agent design, bloats the coordinator's context with raw results, and is a much larger change than needed.
whyWrong.D: An external queue is over-engineering. The SDK already runs subagents in parallel when they are requested in one response.

questions.mindset: Independent subtasks: delegate them in the same response, and reach for the simplest mechanism the framework already has.

questions.stem: A coordinator's prompt tells each research subagent exactly what to do in 25 numbered steps ("1. Search for X. 2. Open the top three results. 3. ..."). The subagents do well on routine topics but stall or return thin results when sources do not fit the script, for example when a key source is a dataset instead of an article. What change to the coordinator's delegation prompts is MOST likely to improve results across varied topics?

options.text: Extend the procedure with extra numbered steps that cover datasets, paywalled sources and other cases seen in failures.
Add a few worked examples of the procedure being followed for different topics so subagents copy the pattern closely.
State the research goal, the expected output format and the quality criteria, and let each subagent choose how to meet them.
Ask each subagent to rate its own confidence at the end and to repeat the whole procedure if the score is low.

questions.explanation: Coordinator prompts should specify **goals and quality criteria** (plus output format and boundaries) rather than step-by-step procedures. This lets subagents adapt when the material does not match an expected path. Anthropic's research system found that clear objectives, output formats and task boundaries were what made delegation work.

whyWrong.A: Adding steps for each failure you have seen just makes a more brittle script. The next unexpected source type will break it again.
whyWrong.B: Examples of the procedure reinforce copying the procedure, which is the rigidity that causes the failures.
whyWrong.D: Self-rating and rerunning the same rigid procedure does not add the ability to adapt. It mostly adds cost and latency.

questions.mindset: Delegate outcomes and quality bars, not scripts, so subagents can adapt.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tools with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.stem: You add a "test-writer" subagent through an AgentDefinition. Two problems appear: the main agent rarely chooses test-writer even for requests like "add unit tests for the parser", and when it does, test-writer sometimes runs shell commands, which your security team forbids for this role. Which configuration change addresses BOTH problems MOST reliably?

options.text: Add "Only use test-writer for testing tasks and never run shell commands" to the main agent's system prompt.
Write a description saying when to use test-writer (writing or extending tests) and set tools to Read, Grep, Glob and Write.
Omit the tools field so test-writer inherits every tool, and add "do not use Bash" to the subagent's own system prompt.
Rename the subagent to unit-test-generator-agent so its purpose is obvious and the model selects it more often.

questions.explanation: The AgentDefinition `description` is what the main agent uses to decide **when** to delegate, so a clear, task-oriented description fixes selection. The `tools` field restricts what the subagent can call. Listing only Read, Grep, Glob and Write removes Bash deterministically, which meets the security requirement. (Leaving `tools` out means the subagent inherits all available tools.)

whyWrong.A: Both concerns stay as instructions the model may not follow. A prompt cannot guarantee that Bash is never used.
whyWrong.C: Omitting tools grants Bash along with everything else, and "do not use Bash" in a prompt has a non-zero failure rate. This also does nothing for selection.
whyWrong.D: A name gives the model a small hint, but the description is the field built for routing. Renaming does nothing about Bash.

questions.mindset: Use the description to steer when a subagent is chosen and the tools list to enforce what it can do; prompts don't enforce.

questions.stem: A coordinator spawns a standard (non-fork) subagent through the Task tool in the Agent SDK. The subagent's AgentDefinition sets only description, prompt and tools, with no optional memory setting. Which statement BEST describes what the subagent starts with?

options.text: It starts with a copy of the coordinator's full conversation so far, including every earlier tool result, so it can continue seamlessly.
It shares a memory store with earlier runs of the same subagent type, so it can build on what those runs found.
It receives the coordinator's tool results but not its system prompt, so it has the data without the coordinator's instructions.
It starts with a fresh context made of its own definition and the Task prompt, and only its final message goes back.

questions.explanation: A standard subagent runs in an **isolated context**. It gets its own system prompt (from its definition), the task prompt the coordinator wrote, and its own tools. It does not get the parent's history or tool results, and it does not share memory between invocations. Only its final message returns to the parent. (Project CLAUDE.md can also be loaded, but conversation state never is.)

whyWrong.A: This is the most common misconception. Standard subagents do not inherit the parent's conversation, which is why context must be passed explicitly.
whyWrong.B: Invocations do not share memory by default. Each spawn starts fresh unless you pass prior results in its prompt. (The optional `memory` field gives a subagent a persistent directory for learnings, but this definition does not set it.)
whyWrong.C: Tool results from the parent are not forwarded automatically. Only what the coordinator writes into the Task prompt arrives.

questions.mindset: Assume a subagent knows nothing except what you hand it.

questions.scenario: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.stem: The support agent has already called get_customer and lookup_order for a return request. It then spawns a "policy-check" subagent with the prompt "Is this return eligible under our policy?" The subagent answers vaguely or asks which item is meant, and resolution stalls. Which TWO of the following would each, on its own, resolve the stall? Choose TWO.

options.text: Set the policy-check subagent's model to inherit so that it receives the coordinator's conversation along with the model setting.
Include the verified customer ID, order ID, purchase date, item category and the customer's stated reason in the Task prompt.
Add a line to the subagent's system prompt telling it to always take the order date and item category into account.
Let the policy-check subagent call get_customer and lookup_order again so that it can rebuild the case details itself.
Have the main agent run the eligibility check itself, because it already holds the order details and the check is small.

questions.explanation: The subagent fails because it never received the case facts: subagents get only what is in the Task prompt. Two independent fixes work. Pass the complete, explicit facts (IDs, date, category, reason) in the prompt (B), or skip delegation altogether: **don't spawn a subagent when the coordinator already holds the needed context** and the task is small (E). Each one removes the context gap on its own; E also avoids extra latency and tokens.

whyWrong.A: `model: inherit` only reuses the parent's model. It does not carry over conversation history.
whyWrong.C: Telling the subagent to consider the order date does not give it the order date. Instructions cannot replace missing data.
whyWrong.D: The prompt contains no customer or order ID, so the subagent cannot even look the case up. Repeating lookups also wastes calls, widens the subagent's tool access and duplicates data the coordinator already verified.

questions.mindset: Either pass the full context explicitly or don't delegate at all; never delegate with a reference the subagent can't resolve.

questions.stem: Yesterday a developer spent two hours in Claude Code on an intermittent authentication bug, in a session named auth-flake. This morning she started two unrelated Claude Code sessions in the same repository. Now she wants to return to the auth-flake conversation with all of its context. What should she do?

options.text: Run claude --continue, which reopens the previous investigation in this repository with its full history.
Open a new session and write "Continue the auth-flake investigation from yesterday" so Claude finds that context.
Run claude --resume auth-flake to reopen that specific named session with its conversation history intact.
Run /compact in a new session with the focus "auth-flake" so that the earlier investigation is summarized into it.

questions.explanation: `--resume <session-name>` continues a **specific** prior conversation by name or ID. Named sessions are made for multi-day investigations like this one.

whyWrong.A: `--continue` picks the **most recent** session in the directory, which is one of this morning's unrelated sessions, not auth-flake.
whyWrong.B: A new session starts with an empty conversation. Mentioning the old one by name does not load its history.
whyWrong.D: `/compact` summarizes the conversation you are already in. It cannot pull in the history of a different session.

questions.mindset: Continue means most recent; resume by name means exactly the conversation you meant.

questions.stem: An agent spent yesterday analyzing a payments module and found three candidate causes of a rounding bug. Overnight, a teammate merged changes to two of the files it analyzed (ledger.py and currency.py). The rest of the analysis is still valid. What is the MOST efficient and reliable way to continue?

options.text: Resume the session and tell the agent that ledger.py and currency.py changed so it re-analyzes just those files.
Resume the session without comment, since the agent will notice the changed files when it next reads them.
Start a brand-new session and have the agent explore the whole payments module from scratch to get a clean baseline.
Resume the session and tell the agent to re-read every file it opened yesterday before it continues with the analysis.

questions.explanation: When most prior context is still valid, **resume**, and **tell the agent which previously analyzed files changed** so it re-analyzes them specifically. This keeps the valuable reasoning and corrects exactly the part that went stale.

whyWrong.B: Nothing guarantees the agent re-reads those files. It may reason from its earlier tool results, which it treats as current, and stale reads quietly corrupt the analysis.
whyWrong.C: Starting over throws away valid analysis and repeats expensive exploration. A fresh start is for when most prior context is stale.
whyWrong.D: This works, but re-reading everything wastes time and context when you already know exactly which two files changed.

questions.mindset: On resume, name what changed: targeted re-analysis beats both blind trust and a full redo.

questions.scenario: You are building a customer support resolution agent using the Claude Agent SDK. It handles returns, billing disputes and account issues through custom MCP tools (get_customer, lookup_order, process_refund, escalate_to_human), targeting 80%+ first-contact resolution while knowing when to escalate.
questions.stem: A billing dispute case was paused for four days while the warehouse inspected a returned item. The original session contains earlier get_customer and lookup_order results showing the order as "in transit" with no refund issued. Since then the item has arrived, been inspected and a partial credit was applied by another team. The agent now needs to finish the case. What is the MOST reliable way to continue?

options.text: Resume the original session as it is, because the full history gives the agent the richest possible context for the case.
Resume the original session and add a message telling the agent to ignore any order status it saw earlier in the conversation.
Fork the original session so the agent can continue on a branch while the original history stays intact for auditing.
Start a new session seeded with a structured summary of verified facts and decisions so far, and have it re-fetch current state.

questions.explanation: When earlier tool results are **stale**, starting a new session with an **injected structured summary** (customer ID, order ID, what was verified, what was decided, what is pending) is more reliable than resuming. The agent then calls the tools again for current order and refund state, instead of reasoning over outdated results that are still in its context.

whyWrong.A: The history is full of out-of-date tool results. A richer context is a worse one when the key facts in it are wrong, and the agent could issue a duplicate refund.
whyWrong.B: The stale results are still in context alongside the correction. An instruction to ignore them is probabilistic, and here money is at stake.
whyWrong.C: A fork copies the same stale history into the new branch, so it has exactly the same problem as resuming.

questions.mindset: Stale tool results poison a resume; carry forward a clean summary and re-fetch the facts.

questions.scenario: You are building developer productivity tools with the Claude Agent SDK. The agent helps engineers explore unfamiliar codebases, understand legacy systems, generate boilerplate and automate repetitive tasks, using the built-in tools (Read, Write, Bash, Grep, Glob) plus MCP servers.
questions.stem: An agent has finished a long analysis of a legacy order-processing service: dependency map, hot paths and test gaps. The team wants to compare two refactoring approaches (extracting a separate pricing service vs. applying a strategy pattern in place). Each approach should build on the same analysis without the other approach's reasoning shaping it. What should the architect do?

options.text: Resume the analysis session and ask the agent to work through both approaches one after the other, then compare them.
Fork the analysis session twice with fork_session and develop one refactoring approach in each independent branch.
Start two new sessions and have each one repeat the full codebase analysis before working on its assigned approach.
Define two custom subagents with AgentDefinitions, give each one approach, and tell both to build on the analysis in the parent context.

questions.explanation: `fork_session` creates a **new session with a copy of the history** up to that point and leaves the original unchanged. Forking twice gives two independent branches from a shared analysis baseline, which is the case it was built for, such as comparing refactoring approaches.

whyWrong.A: Working sequentially in one conversation lets the first approach's reasoning shape the second, which is the contamination the team wants to avoid.
whyWrong.C: Repeating an expensive analysis twice wastes time and tokens, and the two runs may not even produce the same baseline.
whyWrong.D: Custom subagents defined with AgentDefinitions start with a fresh context: they do not inherit the parent's conversation, so "build on the analysis in the parent's context" gives them nothing to build on unless the analysis is pasted into each prompt.

questions.mindset: Shared baseline, divergent exploration: fork the session instead of repeating or mixing work.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about forking an Agent SDK session are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: A fork is a new session that starts with a copy of the original's history, and the original session is left unchanged.
A fork snapshots the working directory, so file edits made in the fork can be thrown away by deleting the fork.
File edits made while working in a fork are real changes on disk, and both the fork and the original see them.
The original and the fork keep sharing one history, so new messages in either branch also appear in the other one.
A fork starts with an empty context, so the original system prompt and history must be passed to it again.

questions.explanation: Sessions hold **conversation history, not the filesystem**. A fork copies the history into a new, independent session with its own ID and leaves the original as it was (A). File changes are not isolated: edits made in a fork happen on the real filesystem and are visible to any session working in that directory (C). If both branches will edit files, isolate them with git worktrees or branches, and use file checkpointing to revert.

whyWrong.B: Forking does not snapshot or sandbox files. Reverting file changes is the job of file checkpointing or git; isolating them needs worktrees or branches.
whyWrong.D: After the fork point the two histories are independent. Later messages in one do not appear in the other.
whyWrong.E: A fork starts *with* a copy of the history. That is its whole purpose. An empty context describes a new session, not a fork.

questions.mindset: A session is the conversation, not the disk: forks isolate reasoning, not files.

questions.stem: A backend service uses the Agent SDK to run many investigation jobs at the same time from the same working directory. Some jobs end with error_max_turns, and operators want to resume any job later, including the failed ones, with its full conversation. What is the MOST reliable way to make that possible?

options.text: On every follow-up, call query with continue enabled so that the SDK reopens the job's own most recent conversation.
Save the final assistant text of each job and send it as the opening prompt of a new session when the job is resumed.
Store the session_id from each job's ResultMessage with the job record, and pass it as the resume option when resuming.
When a job needs resuming, open the most recently modified session file in the project's session directory and resume it.

questions.explanation: Every `ResultMessage` carries a `session_id`, **including error results** such as `error_max_turns`. Saving it with the job record and passing it as `resume` reopens exactly that job's conversation, whatever else ran in the same directory.

whyWrong.A: `continue` picks the most recent session in the directory, not "this job's" session. With jobs running concurrently it will often pick the wrong one.
whyWrong.B: This starts a new conversation with only a fragment of the context. Failed jobs may not even have useful final text.
whyWrong.D: "Most recently modified" races with other concurrent jobs, the same flaw as continue, plus fragile file handling.

questions.mindset: Track sessions by explicit ID, never by 'most recent'.

questions.scenario: You are integrating Claude Code into your CI/CD pipeline. It runs automated code reviews, generates test cases and posts feedback on pull requests, and you want actionable feedback with few false positives.
questions.stem: A nightly CI job runs claude -p to analyze the test suite and records its session ID. The team now wants two follow-up runs on the same runner, each in its own git worktree: one tries property-based tests, the other example-based tests. Each must start from the nightly analysis without seeing the other's reasoning, and the analysis session must stay unchanged for tomorrow's comparison. What should the follow-up runs do?

options.text: Run each with claude -p --resume <analysis-id> --fork-session, so each run branches into its own new session from the analysis.
Run each with claude -p --resume <analysis-id>, one after the other, so that both strategies build directly on the analysis session.
Run each with claude -p --continue, so that each one automatically picks up the most recent analysis conversation on the runner.
Paste the analysis's final text into two fresh claude -p runs, because the CLI has no way to branch a saved session into a new one.

questions.explanation: `--fork-session` used with `--resume` creates a **new session ID** that starts with a copy of the analysis history, and the original session is left unchanged. Two forked runs give two independent branches from one shared baseline, which is the CLI form of `fork_session`. The separate git worktrees matter too: forks branch the conversation, not the filesystem, so file edits need their own isolation.

whyWrong.B: Plain `--resume` reuses the same session. The second run would see the first strategy's reasoning, and the analysis session would no longer be the clean baseline the team wants to keep.
whyWrong.C: `--continue` reopens the most recent conversation, which after the first run is that run's session, not the analysis. It also adds to whichever session it opens instead of branching.
whyWrong.D: The premise is false: `--fork-session` exists for this. A pasted final answer also drops the tool results and detail from the analysis.

questions.mindset: Shared baseline, divergent branches: resume with a fork, never by extending the baseline itself.

questions.scenario: You are building a multi-agent research system with the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates to specialized subagents: a web search agent, a document analysis agent, a synthesis agent and a report generation agent. The system produces comprehensive, cited research reports.
questions.stem: Midway through a large research run, the host process crashes. Six of ten research subagents had already finished, and the coordinator had been running for over an hour. Restarting from scratch would be expensive. Which TWO design choices would MOST reliably let the system recover and finish without redoing completed work? Choose TWO.

options.text: Re-run the whole pipeline after a crash, since partial results from an interrupted run can't be trusted to be consistent.
Re-spawn the same subagent types after restart, since each one remembers the work it finished in its earlier invocation.
Have each subagent write its findings to a known location (a manifest), and on restart load and inject them into prompts.
Raise maxTurns and the budget limits so the run finishes sooner and is less likely to be cut off by a crash next time.
Capture the coordinator's session_id when the run starts, so that after a restart its conversation can be resumed by ID.

questions.explanation: Recovery needs durable state outside the process. (C) A manifest of completed subagent outputs lets the coordinator reload finished work, inject it into later prompts and re-delegate only the unfinished tasks. (E) Sessions are saved to disk, so the coordinator's conversation can be resumed by its captured `session_id`. Together they rebuild both the coordinator's reasoning and the subagents' results.

whyWrong.A: Throwing away six completed results is the costly outcome the design is supposed to avoid. Completed, persisted outputs are reusable.
whyWrong.B: A re-spawned subagent starts with a fresh context and knows nothing about its earlier run's findings. Subagents do not share memory between invocations by default, and even the optional `memory` directory is for learnings, not a reliable record of task outputs.
whyWrong.D: Limits on turns and budget do not prevent crashes or save progress. Raising them only removes cost guardrails.

questions.mindset: Make progress durable and addressable: persist outputs and session IDs, then resume instead of restarting.
